source.title: Retrospective on ‘GPT-4 Predictions’ After the Release of GPT-4

record.tranche_reason: The post retrospectively compares a downstream-performance prediction with GPT-4's reported MMLU result. It does not reproduce the original loss-scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The post discusses and uses scaling-law claims, but reports no parameter, token, or compute sweep and no direct measurement of held-out pretraining loss. Its relevant result is the predicted-versus-reported MMLU accuracy. Other reported model properties and performance predictions do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The post compares one MMLU accuracy predicted from scaling-law loss estimates plus a linear loss–MMLU fit against GPT-4's reported score. This bears weakly on V6 and on nothing else. No loss is measured; GPT-4's loss is back-inferred from MMLU.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author says scaling laws and simple quantitative methods can predict general LM performance in the short term, and that long-term (>5 years) prediction is much harder because of algorithmic advances and emergent nonlinear capabilities. He also stresses that many of his predictions were inaccurate (compute, parameters, modality, context length) and attributes the MMLU underprediction partly to unmodelled algorithmic advances.
record.recipe_differences: This is a retrospective evaluation of a prior prediction, using a loss–MMLU relationship and scaling-law estimates; it does not run a model-scaling experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The author notes that algorithmic advances and nonlinear changes in specific capabilities can affect prediction accuracy.
record.problems: GPT-4's training details are limited; the loss estimate is uncertain, and the post evaluates only one downstream benchmark prediction. The MMLU comparison does not directly establish scaling of held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported result directly measures one of the claim versions.

untested.parts: No loss measurements across parameters, tokens or compute.
No measured loss of a large run compared with a small-run fit. GPT-4's loss is inferred from MMLU, not measured.
No compute-optimal allocation test. Chinchilla tables are used only to back out a parameter estimate.
Only one model and one benchmark, with uncertain inputs. No other tasks or scales.

record.verdict_notes: This is an informal LessWrong post, not peer reviewed. The GPT-4 loss of 1.85 is derived by inverting the loss–MMLU regression on the actual MMLU score, so it is circular and not evidence for V1 or V2. OpenAI's quoted predictable-scaling claim and its 1.2 bit/word codebase loss are cited results, not this study's. The compute, training-time, GPU, parameter and context-length predictions do not measure any version.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law loss measurements across parameters, tokens, or compute.
No comparison of loss predictions from small runs with measured losses of runs orders of magnitude larger.
No compute-budget sweep or test of the loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
No comparison of architectures at a fixed parameter count.
No test of power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Only one downstream benchmark prediction for GPT-4 is evaluated; other tasks, models, and scales are not tested.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across setups or fitting choices.

rows.subject: GPT-4
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained transformer; fine-tuning and RLHF are also mentioned
rows.operation_detail: Compared the post's MMLU accuracy prediction with GPT-4's reported MMLU accuracy.
rows.note: The post reports an 8.1% percent error and describes the prediction as higher than predicted in accuracy.
rows.check: Recorded as observed. The prediction (79.4%) undershot the reported 86.4% by 7 points. On error rate it was 20.6% predicted vs 13.6% actual, about 51% more errors, as the author concedes in comments. The 'baseline' is a prediction, not a control. The input compute was underestimated about 4x (5.63e24 vs 2.2e25). So the test does not cleanly isolate whether the scaling-law step or the loss→MMLU step failed.

relationships.condition: GPT-4 on MMLU, predicted from estimated loss via a linear loss–MMLU fit
relationships.reason: The direction and the new-record call were right, but the score was underpredicted by 7 points (about 51% more predicted errors). Inputs such as compute were off about 4x. Single data point (r1).
relationships.display_finding: The forecast correctly predicted improvement and a new record but underestimated MMLU by 7 points, implying about 51% excess predicted errors, while inputs such as compute were off by about 4×.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The predicted accuracy was 79.4% and the reported result was 86.4%, which the post presents as a fairly accurate short-term prediction (r1).
